overview:
Panama is the narrow S-shaped country that joins Central and South America, touching Costa Rica in the west and Colombia in the east. At its slimmest the land between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean is only about 50 kilometers wide, and through that gap runs the Panama Canal, one of the great engineering works of the world.

About 4.4 million people live in Panama, speaking Spanish, with English and Indigenous languages such as Ngäbere and Guna also heard. Panama City, the capital, faces the Pacific with a skyline of glass towers rising beside a Spanish colonial old town.

Panama is a presidential republic. Because ships from everywhere pass through it, the country runs on trade, banking and shipping; more merchant ships fly Panama's flag than any other country's. Rainforest still covers much of the land, and the canal's watershed is protected because the canal needs the rain the forest helps hold.
landAndNature: Panama runs east to west rather than north to south, so from parts of the country the sun rises over the Pacific. A mountain spine divides the wet Caribbean side from the drier Pacific side, topped by Volcán Barú at 3,475 meters, from which both oceans can be seen on a clear day. The Darién, a roadless tangle of rainforest and swamp on the Colombian border, is the one gap in the highway that otherwise runs from Alaska to Argentina. Because Panama formed a land bridge about three million years ago, animals from two continents mixed here: jaguars, tapirs, sloths, capybaras and more than 1,000 bird species, including the huge harpy eagle, the national bird. Coral reefs and 1,500 islands line both coasts.
peopleAndCulture: Panama's people are a blend of Indigenous, Spanish, African and Caribbean heritage, with communities descended from West Indian workers who built the canal and railway. The Guna of the San Blas islands govern themselves and are known for molas, layered cloth panels stitched into bold patterns of birds, fish and geometric shapes. The pollera, an embroidered ruffled dress worn with gold jewelry and hair combs, appears at Carnival, the biggest party of the year. Sancocho, a chicken and root-vegetable soup seasoned with the herb culantro, is the comfort food. Baseball is the top sport, and Panama has sent many players to the major leagues; Roberto Durán became one of boxing's greatest champions. Salsa star Rubén Blades is from Panama City.
history: Indigenous peoples fished and farmed here for thousands of years. Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the isthmus in 1513 and became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas. Panama became Spain's treasure route: silver from Peru crossed by mule trail to be shipped to Spain, attracting pirates who burned Panama City in 1671. Panama joined Colombia after independence from Spain in 1821. France tried and failed to dig a canal in the 1880s, losing tens of thousands of workers to disease. In 1903 Panama separated from Colombia with United States backing, and the United States built the canal, opened in 1914, at the cost of about 5,600 more lives. A 1977 treaty handed the canal to Panama on December 31, 1999.
funFacts: A ship crossing the canal is lifted about 26 meters up into a lake by locks, then lowered back to the other ocean.
Because of Panama's curve, ships sailing from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travel southeast.
The Darién Gap is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, leaving about 100 kilometers with no road at all.
More ships are registered in Panama than in any other country, though most never come near it.
Panama's golden frog, a national symbol, waves its hands to signal to others over the roar of streams.
